findings.title: Large animated GIF uploads are converted to a single-frame image
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.optimize` chooses the animated GIF path by matching the `from` path against `/\.GIF$/i`, but this call passes `tempfile.path`, whose Rack/Tempfile-generated name normally has no `.gif` extension. Consequently, even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled, an oversized GIF takes `downsize_instructions`, which uses `convert #{from}[0]` and writes only the first frame. Uploading a GIF large enough to trigger downsizing therefore silently destroys its animation; pass the original filename/format through to the optimizer or select the animated path from MIME/image metadata rather than the temporary path suffix.

findings.title: Attachment size settings are no longer enforced by the upload client
findings.body: The maximum is now unconditionally 10 MB, even when `type` is `attachment`. This ignores `max_attachment_size_kb` (and also caps installations configured to permit image uploads larger than 10 MB), whereas the previous code used the configured per-type limit. Users can now spend time uploading attachments that the server/site policy rejects, and sites that intentionally allow files above 10 MB cannot select them at all. Keep the configured attachment limit for attachments and use a separately defined pre-downsize input limit for images.

findings.title: API URL uploads are newly limited to 10 MB regardless of site configuration
findings.body: Remote API uploads previously downloaded up to `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`; replacing that with `10.megabytes` causes a configured image limit above 10 MB to be ignored before downsizing can run. An API client supplying a URL to a valid, configured-allowed 20 MB image will now receive a failed upload/download instead of the image being processed. Use a configurable source-file ceiling that is at least compatible with the site's allowed image size (or document and expose the new API limit).
